text: A northern French county of cloth towns and tapestries, created as a royal appanage and later held by Burgundy and Spain before returning to France.

[[e:arras|Arras]] was a major cloth and banking town, and its tapestries became so famous that 'arras' meant a wall hanging in English and Italian. Count [[e:robert-ii-count-of-artois|Robert II]] was killed at [[e:kortrijk|Courtrai]] in 1302, and his daughter [[e:mahaut-countess-of-artois|Mahaut]] defended her inheritance against her nephew [[e:robert-iii-of-artois|Robert III]]. In 1384 Artois passed with [[s:county-of-flanders|Flanders]] to [[e:philip-the-bold|Philip the Bold]], joining the [[s:burgundian-state|Burgundian State]].

Wei controlled the populous north. Military agricultural colonies, the tuntian, fed its armies, and the [[e:nine-rank-system|Nine-Rank system]] for recommending officials entrenched great families. The court of the Cao family fostered the [[e:jian-an-poetry|Jian'an]] poets. Wei fought [[s:shu-han|Shu Han]] and [[s:eastern-wu|Eastern Wu]], absorbed [[s:gongsun-yan|Gongsun Yan]] in 238 and received envoys from Queen [[e:himiko|Himiko]] of the Wa in [[e:japan|Japan]].
A formidable south-eastern nation, allies of the British and enemies of the French, who after removal built a self-governing republic in Indian Territory.

In 1112 the heiress [[e:douce-i-countess-of-provence|Douce]] married [[e:ramon-berenguer-iii-of-barcelona|Ramon Berenguer III of Barcelona]], bringing Catalan counts who fostered troubadour culture and [[e:mediterranean|Mediterranean]] trade. [[e:ramon-berenguer-iv-count-of-provence|Raymond Berengar IV]]'s daughter [[e:beatrice-of-provence|Beatrice]] married [[e:charles-i-of-anjou|Charles of Anjou]] in 1246, and the Angevin counts, also kings of [[e:naples|Naples]], ruled from [[e:aix-en-provence|Aix]] and Naples. The popes settled at [[e:avignon|Avignon]], on the county's edge, in the 14th century.
The city-republic at the heart of the 'joyful March', whose courtly culture under the da Camino lords was praised by Dante.
The Habsburg duchy at the heart of modern Slovenia, centred on Ljubljana, a borderland between the German, Slovene and Italian worlds.

In 1453 [[e:frederick-iii-holy-roman-emperor|Emperor Frederick III]], himself a [[s:county-of-habsburg|Habsburg]], confirmed the [[e:privilegium-maius|Privilegium Maius]], raising [[e:austria|Austria]] to an archduchy. The [[s:archduchy-of-austria|Archduchy of Austria]] became the core of the [[e:habsburg-dynasty|Habsburg]] monarchy, the [[s:austrian-empire|Austrian Empire]] and, ultimately, the modern [[s:first-austrian-republic|Republic of Austria]].

Under the testament of [[e:boleslaw-iii-wrymouth|Boleslaw III]] in 1138, his son [[e:mieszko-iii-the-old|Mieszko III the Old]] received Greater [[e:poland|Poland]], with [[e:poznan|Poznan]] and [[e:gniezno|Gniezno]], the cradle of the [[e:piast-dynasty|Piast]] state. For much of the next century the duchy was contested between Mieszko's descendants and was at times divided between Poznan and [[e:kalisz|Kalisz]].
The Norman duchy of Robert Guiscard, which drove the Byzantines out of southern Italy and laid the groundwork for the Kingdom of Sicily.

Around 1566 [[e:abu-bakr-ibn-muhammad|Abu Bakr ibn Muhammad]] al-Majati founded a zawiya at Dila in the [[e:middle-atlas|Middle Atlas]], among [[e:sanhaja|Sanhaja Berber]] tribes. It became a renowned centre of [[e:sufism|Sufi]] teaching and scholarship, attracting students and gifts, and grew wealthy and influential as the [[s:saadi-sultanate|Saadi Sultanate]] weakened after 1603.
The leading city of north-central Veracruz, renowned for the Pyramid of the Niches and for its many ballcourts carved with scenes of sacrifice.
Argolid city-state whose sanctuary of Asclepius became the most famous healing centre of the Greek world, with its magnificent theatre.

[[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] captured the island again in 1803 and the [[e:treaty-of-paris-1814|Treaty of Paris]] of 1814 ceded it to [[e:britain|Britain]], creating the [[s:colony-of-saint-lucia|Colony of Saint Lucia]]. French law, place names, [[e:catholicism|Catholicism]] and the French-based [[e:antillean-creole|Kwéyòl]] language remained a lasting legacy of the French period.

Protected by mountains, the fertile [[e:sichuan|Sichuan]] basin escaped the wars of the north and prospered from [[e:rice|rice]], [[e:silk|silk]], salt and [[e:tea|tea]]. Many [[s:later-tang|Tang]] officials and literati took refuge at [[e:chengdu|Chengdu]], among them the poet [[e:wei-zhuang|Wei Zhuang]], who served as chief minister. The Huajian anthology of song lyrics was compiled there in 940, after the dynasty, but reflects the court culture it fostered.

In 1903 the colony was divided into [[s:gabon-french-colony|Gabon]], [[s:middle-congo|Middle Congo]] and Ubangi-Shari-[[e:chad|Chad]], and in 1910 these were organised as [[s:french-equatorial-africa|French Equatorial Africa]], with [[e:brazzaville|Brazzaville]] as capital. The concession system left a lasting legacy of depopulation and distrust.
Small Westphalian republic whose January 1933 election the Nazis used as a showcase just before Hitler came to power.

After the 1930 election, [[e:getulio-vargas|Getúlio Vargas]] of [[e:rio-grande-do-sul|Rio Grande do Sul]] led the Revolution of 1930, which deposed President [[e:washington-luis|Washington Luís]] and opened the [[s:second-brazilian-republic|Second Brazilian Republic]]. Its federal structure and the power of the states left a lasting mark on Brazilian politics.

British and Ottoman forces landed in 1801, and the French capitulated at [[e:cairo|Cairo]] and [[e:alexandria|Alexandria]] that year. The collapse of [[e:mamluk|Mamluk]] power paved the way for [[s:egypt-under-muhammad-ali|Egypt under Muhammad Ali]].
The short-lived British Crown colony around the Kimberley diamond fields, the cradle of South Africa's mining industry.

Gela reached its peak under the tyrants Cleander and [[e:hippocrates-of-gela|Hippocrates]], who around 495 BCE dominated much of eastern [[e:sicily|Sicily]], and under [[e:gelon|Gelon]], who seized [[s:syracuse|Syracuse]] in 485 BCE and moved half of Gela's people there. Its farmland produced grain and horses, and its terracotta workshops and coins with a man-headed bull were renowned. The playwright [[e:aeschylus|Aeschylus]] died there in 456 BCE.

In 1776 [[e:charles-iii-of-spain|Charles III]] made [[e:buenos-aires|Buenos Aires]] the capital of the new [[s:viceroyalty-of-the-rio-de-la-plata|Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata]], which absorbed the governorate. The port's growing importance laid the foundations for [[e:argentina|Argentina's]] later dominance in the region.
A Turkic dynasty from Ghazni whose sultan Mahmud raided deep into India and whose court fostered Persian literature, including Ferdowsi's Shahnameh.
Around 830 BCE [[e:hazael|Hazael]] of [[s:aram-damascus|Aram-Damascus]] besieged and destroyed Gath; the siege trench he dug has been excavated. The city never recovered its leading role.

In the [[e:late-bronze-age|Late Bronze Age]] local kings ruled as [[e:vassal|vassals]] of the [[s:egyptian-empire-new-kingdom|Egyptian Empire New Kingdom]]. [[e:thutmose-iii|Thutmose III]] lists Gezer among his conquests, its kings Milkilu and Yapahu wrote [[e:amarna-letters|Amarna letters]], and the [[e:merneptah-stele|Merneptah Stele]] boasts that Gezer was seized. The Gezer calendar, an early [[e:hebrew|Hebrew]] inscription, was found there.
The Karnataka dynasty famous for the intricately carved temples of Belur, Halebidu and Somanathapura.

In the 17th century BCE [[e:hattusili-i|Hattusili I]] of the [[s:hittite-empire|Hittite Empire]] crossed the [[e:euphrates|Euphrates]], burned Hahhum and carried its gods to [[e:hattusa|Hattusa]], boasting that he had surpassed [[e:sargon-of-akkad|Sargon of Akkad]]. The city does not reappear as a kingdom.

Hlubi chiefs ruled over [[e:cattle|cattle]]-herding homesteads, and their royal house was famed for rainmaking. Around 1818 the Hlubi were attacked by the [[s:swazi-kingdom|Ngwane]] and later the [[s:zulu-kingdom|Zulu Kingdom]]; one section under [[e:mpangazitha|Mpangazitha]] fled onto the highveld and fought in the wars of the 1820s. Others later settled in [[s:natal-colony|Natal]] under [[e:langalibalele|Langalibalele]], a renowned rainmaker.

[[e:ahilyabai-holkar|Ahilyabai Holkar]] (ruled 1767–95) became renowned for just administration and for rebuilding temples and ghats across [[e:india|India]], from [[s:kingdom-of-kashi|Kashi]] to [[e:somnath-temple|Somnath]]. [[e:yashwant-rao-holkar|Yashwant Rao Holkar]] fought the British in 1804–05, but after defeat at [[e:battle-of-mahidpur|Mahidpur]] in 1817 the [[e:treaty-of-mandsaur|Treaty of Mandsaur]] made Indore a protected state, and the capital moved to Indore. The [[e:cotton|cotton]] trade made Indore a commercial city; [[e:tukoji-rao-holkar-iii|Tukoji Rao III]] abdicated in 1926 after a murder scandal.

Ituraean rulers were also high priests of a local cult, and their warriors were renowned [[e:archery|archers]] later serving in Roman armies. [[e:strabo|Strabo]] describes them as brigands raiding the [[e:caravan-trade|caravan routes]]. Ptolemy made peace with [[e:pompey|Pompey]] in 64 BCE and kept his principality as a Roman client.

The country's nuclear programme led to [[e:sanctions|sanctions]], the 2015 nuclear deal and the US withdrawal from it in 2018, and in 2025 to open war with [[s:kingdom-of-israel|Israel]]. [[e:iran|Iran's]] oil economy, regional alliances and internal dissent continue to shape the state.
A Mongol dynasty that ruled Iraq and Azerbaijan after the Ilkhanate, whose court at Baghdad and Tabriz fostered a golden age of Persian painting.
Inland county at the heart of Estonia, conquered in the early 13th century and later a key holding of the Livonian Order.
Farming city on the west coast of Rhodes, one of the island's three ancient cities, whose terraced streets survive in remarkable condition.
The first Christian kingdom in Iberia after the Muslim conquest, born at Covadonga and seen as the cradle of the Reconquista.
Dorian port city on a Carian peninsula, home of Praxiteles's Aphrodite, the astronomer Eudoxus and a renowned school of medicine.
A kingdom of the highlands between Rwanda and Uganda, remembered for its queen Kitami and as the cradle of the Nyabingi spirit cult.

The mugabe (king) presided over a society divided between the [[e:cattle|cattle]]-owning [[e:bahima|Bahima]] and the farming [[e:bairu|Bairu]], with power and prestige tied to herds of long-horned cattle. The royal drum [[e:bagyendanwa|Bagyendanwa]] embodied the kingship. Rule was loose, relying on chiefs and the king's cattle camps. Under [[e:ntare-v|Ntare V]] in the late 19th century Ankole extended its influence over neighbouring states.

Nri's influence waned from the 18th century as the [[s:aro-confederacy|Aro Confederacy]] and slave trading reshaped [[e:igboland|Igboland]]. In 1911 British colonial officials forced the [[e:eze-nri|Eze Nri]] to renounce his ritual powers. The title survives as a traditional office in [[e:anambra-state|Anambra State]], and Nri is remembered as a cradle of [[e:igbo-people|Igbo]] culture.

Bamum came under [[s:kamerun|German Kamerun]] around 1902 and then [[s:french-cameroon|French Cameroon]] after the [[e:first-world-war|First World War]]. The French curtailed [[e:ibrahim-njoya|Njoya]]'s power in the 1920s and exiled him in 1931. The dynasty survives as a sultanate at [[e:foumban|Foumban]], whose palace houses a renowned museum.
The German kingdom at the heart of the Holy Roman Empire, an elective monarchy whose kings claimed the imperial crown for more than eight centuries.
The south Indian kingdom of the Wodeyars that became a formidable military power under Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan.
Central European kingdom centred on Prague, home of Charles IV's golden age and the Hussite revolution, and the crown at the heart of the Thirty Years War.
The sacred city of the Yoruba, cradle of their royal dynasties and home of some of Africa's finest naturalistic bronze and terracotta sculpture.

Rivalries with neighbouring courts wore the kingdom down, and in 1891 a coalition of neighbouring courts led by the [[s:kingdom-of-badung|Kingdom of Badung]] and the [[s:kingdom-of-tabanan|Kingdom of Tabanan]] conquered Mengwi and divided its lands. [[e:pura-taman-ayun|Taman Ayun]] is now part of a [[e:unesco-world-heritage-site|UNESCO World Heritage]] cultural landscape.

After the [[e:october-revolution|October Revolution]], the [[e:tashkent-soviet|Tashkent Soviet]], dominated by Russian settlers, excluded Muslims from power. In November 1917 the Fourth Extraordinary Regional Muslim Congress met in [[e:kokand|Kokand]] and proclaimed the Turkestan Autonomy within a future democratic Russian federation.
A northern Mesopotamian kingdom of the Mari age, centred on Tell al-Rimah, whose queen Iltani left a remarkable archive of letters.
Kussara, the Anatolian kingdom of Pithana and Anitta, who forged the first large state of central Anatolia and paved the way for the Hittites.
A Rathore Rajput state of Rajasthan celebrated for the Kishangarh school of painting and its iconic image of Bani Thani.

The [[e:maharaja|Maharajas]] served as Mughal mansabdars and later accepted British protection in 1818. The court became a centre of [[e:krishna|Krishna]] devotion and art: under Raja [[e:sawant-singh|Sawant Singh]], the poet Nagari Das, painters such as [[e:nihal-chand|Nihal Chand]] created the elongated, lyrical Kishangarh style, epitomised by the portrait known as [[e:bani-thani|Bani Thani]]. It was a fifteen-gun salute state.
Central Balinese kingdom that chose Dutch protection in 1900 and whose princes at Ubud fostered Bali's modern arts.
The leading kingdom of eastern Tibet (Kham), renowned for the Derge printing house and as the cradle of the 19th-century Rime religious movement.

Under [[e:tem-binoka|Tem Binoka]], who succeeded in the 1870s, Abemama was an [[e:autocracy|autocracy]]: the king controlled land, labour and trade, and he dealt directly with European ships, selling copra and buying goods for himself. Foreign residents were strictly limited. [[e:robert-louis-stevenson|Robert Louis Stevenson]], who stayed on the island in 1889, described Binoka in 'In the South Seas' as a shrewd and formidable ruler. Little else is documented in detail.
The autonomous republic of the Karakalpak people on the lower Amu Darya, now part of Uzbekistan and at the heart of the Aral Sea disaster.

The Maharaos ruled the fertile [[e:chambal-river|Chambal]] valley. In the late 18th century the regent [[e:zalim-singh-jhala|Zalim Singh Jhala]] dominated the state, and in 1838 the British created [[s:jhalawar-state|Jhalawar]] for his descendants out of Kota lands. The court fostered the Kota school of painting, noted for its hunting scenes. It was a seventeen-gun salute state.
A semi-independent principality on the middle Euphrates whose governors claimed ancient descent and boasted of introducing honeybees to their land.

The federation had no prince; decisions were taken by assemblies of the tribes, and [[e:thietmar-of-merseburg|Thietmar of Merseburg]] describes the temple of [[e:radegast|Radegast]] ([[e:svarozic|Svarożic]]) at [[e:rethra|Rethra]], whose priests consulted oracles. Remarkably, [[e:henry-ii-holy-roman-emperor|Emperor Henry II]] allied with the pagan Lutici against the Christian Polish ruler Bolesław I, causing scandal among churchmen.

The king ruled through appointed officials and controlled the great market at Saqqa, where traders from the north exchanged cloth, salt and metal goods for gold, [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]], civet, [[e:coffee-economy|coffee]] and slaves. The dynasty adopted [[e:islam|Islam]], and [[e:abba-bagibo|Abba Bagibo]] married into the royal families of neighbouring states. Muslim merchants, the jabarti, played a large role in its economy.

Around 400 BCE La Venta was abandoned and many monuments were damaged. The [[e:olmecs|Olmec]] heartland lost its leading role, but La Venta's art, ritual and ideas of kingship passed into [[e:epi-olmec-culture|Epi-Olmec]], Maya and other later traditions.

After the [[e:ludowingians|Ludowingians]] died out with [[e:henry-raspe|Henry Raspe]] in 1247, the [[e:war-of-the-thuringian-succession|War of the Thuringian Succession]] gave [[e:thuringia|Thuringia]] to the [[e:house-of-wettin|Wettin]] [[e:henry-iii-margrave-of-meissen|Henry the Illustrious]] of [[e:meissen|Meissen]] in 1264, while [[e:hesse|Hesse]] broke away. The landgraviate merged with Wettin lands, ending as a separate unit in 1440.
The early Tai-Lao principality at the meeting of the Mekong and Nam Khan, the site of Luang Prabang and the cradle of the kingdom of Lan Xang.

The Thakore Sahibs ruled a territory of [[e:cotton|cotton]] farms with a port on the Gulf of [[s:cutch-state|Kutch]]. [[e:waghji-ii|Waghji]] and [[e:lakhdhirji-waghji|Lakhdhirji]] in the late 19th and early 20th centuries built a light railway, tramway and Navlakhi port and fostered local industry. It was an eleven-gun salute state.
The Carolingian frontier zone south and east of the Pyrenees, the cradle of the Catalan counties and of Catalonia itself.

The [[e:house-of-wettin|Wettins]] promoted German settlement among the [[s:sorbs|Sorbs]] and founded towns such as [[e:leipzig|Leipzig]] and [[e:dresden|Dresden]]. The discovery of [[e:silver|silver]] at [[e:freiberg|Freiberg]] around 1168 made the margraves wealthy; [[e:otto-the-rich|Otto the Rich]] used it to fortify his lands. [[e:henry-iii-margrave-of-meissen|Henry the Illustrious]] added the [[s:landgraviate-of-thuringia|Landgraviate of Thuringia]] in 1264, making the Wettins a leading princely house.
The northern Nguni paramountcy of Dingiswayo, whose military reorganisation and patronage of the young Shaka paved the way for the Zulu Kingdom.

The Mengujekids were patrons of Persian culture and architecture. [[e:fakhr-al-din-bahramshah|Fakhr al-Din Bahramshah of Erzincan]], who ruled for some sixty years, received the dedication of [[e:nizami-ganjavi|Nizami's]] poem [[e:makhzan-al-asrar|Makhzan al-Asrar]]. In 1228-1229 [[e:ahmad-shah-of-divrigi|Ahmad Shah of Divrigi]] and his wife [[e:turan-malik|Turan Malik]] built the [[e:divrigi-great-mosque-and-hospital|Great Mosque and Hospital of Divrigi]], whose carved stone portals are among the most extraordinary in medieval Islamic art. Their towns had large Armenian and Greek populations.

Kings ruled through royal kin and councillors over [[e:chiefdom|chiefdoms]] of [[e:cattle|cattle]]-herding and cereal-farming homesteads. The [[e:mpondomise|Mpondomise]] were renowned as rainmakers and were respected by neighbouring peoples for their ritual standing. In the 19th century they were caught between the [[e:mpondo|Mpondo]], the [[e:thembu|Thembu]] and incoming [[e:mfengu|Mfengu]] and [[e:sotho-people|Sotho]] groups, and the kingdom was often divided between rival branches.

Kings ruled from large courts with spacious audience halls, supported by tribute in food, [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] and labour from subject peoples. Mangbetu craftsmen were renowned for ironwork, pottery and carved figures, and the elite shaped infants' skulls into an elongated form. The botanist [[e:georg-schweinfurth|Georg Schweinfurth]] described the court of King [[e:munza|Munza]] in 1870 in vivid detail.

Its palace complexes are decorated with intricate geometric step-fret mosaics made of thousands of cut stones fitted without mortar, unlike anything elsewhere in [[e:mesoamerica|Mesoamerica]]. Cruciform tombs lie beneath the courts. Mitla served as a religious centre and was linked politically with the [[s:zaachila|Zapotec kingdom of Zaachila]], while sharing [[e:mixtecs|Mixtec]] artistic influences.

Their main centre was [[e:marruvium|Marruvium]] on the lake shore. [[e:roman-empire|Romans]] regarded the Marsi as experts in magic, healing and snake-charming, linked to the goddess [[e:angitia|Angitia]], whose grove stood by the lake. They were renowned as soldiers; a Roman saying held that no one had ever triumphed over the Marsi or without them. They lived from farming, fishing and herding.

In 85 to 86 CE the Nasamones rose against Roman tax collectors and defeated the governor of [[s:numidia|Numidia]], but were then crushed by the [[s:roman-empire|Roman Empire]], and [[e:domitian|Domitian]] boasted that he had forbidden them to exist. Survivors were absorbed by other Libyan groups.

Nobadia's kings received Roman [[e:subsidy|subsidies]] to guard the frontier and fought the [[s:blemmyes|Blemmyes]]; [[e:silko|King Silko]], in a Greek inscription at [[e:kalabsha|Kalabsha]], boasted of driving them from the [[e:nile|Nile]] valley in the 5th century. The capital was [[e:faras|Faras]] (Pachoras). Around 543 a Miaphysite mission led by the priest Julian, backed by Empress [[e:theodora-wife-of-justinian-i|Theodora]], converted the court, and churches, Coptic and Greek literacy followed.
Osroene, the kingdom of Edessa in upper Mesopotamia, cradle of Syriac literature and one of the earliest centres of Christianity.
The Oghuz Turkic state of the lower Syr Darya and Aral steppe, cradle of the Seljuks and of the Turkmen.
The Franconian margraviate of the Hohenzollerns, ruled from Kulmbach and Bayreuth and made a rococo showcase by Margravine Wilhelmine.
A Franconian church principality on the Altmühl, founded on the see of Saint Willibald, that became a showcase of Catholic Baroque.

In the mid-4th century BCE the city was rebuilt on a terrace of [[e:mount-mycale|Mycale]] with a strict grid; Alexander dedicated its temple of [[e:athena-polias|Athena Polias]]. It passed to [[e:rome|Rome]] in 133 BCE. As the [[e:buyuk-menderes-river|Maeander]] silted its harbour, Priene declined, leaving its ruins remarkably intact.
The Soviet-backed government led by Kim Il Sung that ruled northern Korea from 1946 and laid the groundwork for the North Korean state.
The Catholic line of the Ries counts of Oettingen, raised to princes in 1774, whose court at Wallerstein kept a renowned orchestra.
Small inland city of the north-eastern Peloponnese, renowned for its steadfast loyalty to Sparta and its long siege by Agesilaus.
The leading city-state of the northern Swahili coast in the 17th and 18th centuries, ruled by the Nabhani dynasty and a cradle of Swahili poetry.

[[e:nekhen|Nekhen]] was the cult centre of [[e:horus|Horus]], the falcon god later embodied by every Egyptian king. Its Tomb 100, the 'Painted Tomb', bears the earliest known Egyptian wall painting, with boats, hunting scenes and a figure smiting captives. Excavations have revealed an oval ceremonial court and an elite cemetery with buried animals, including elephants, hippopotami and baboons, signs of an ambitious ruling ideology.
A confederation of Aymara-speaking peoples in the southern Bolivian highlands, renowned as warriors and later linked to the silver mines of Potosí.

Archaeology shows a landscape of local [[e:chiefdom|chiefdoms]] around [[e:quito|Quito]] and its valleys, with farming of [[e:maize|maize]] and [[e:potato|potatoes]] and markets where goods from the coast and [[e:amazon|Amazon]] were traded. [[e:juan-de-velasco|Velasco]]'s account of a centralised kingdom with a line of Shyri kings has no support from earlier chronicles and is widely regarded as legend, though it became a cornerstone of Ecuadorian national identity.

In January 1869 officers voted to elect [[e:enomoto-takeaki|Enomoto]] as president, with other posts filled by election, an unprecedented step in [[e:japan|Japan]]. The regime sought recognition from foreign powers as a de facto authority and asked to develop Ezo under a Tokugawa lord, but received only cautious neutrality.
A settlement founded by Lord Selkirk at the forks of the Red and Assiniboine rivers, cradle of the Métis nation and of the province of Manitoba.

The [[e:audiencia|Audiencia]] was headed by a president. Its economy rested on textile workshops called obrajes, which used indigenous labour to produce woollen cloth sold across the [[s:andecavi|Andes]], and on [[e:hacienda|haciendas]]. [[e:guayaquil|Guayaquil]] was the main port and shipbuilding centre. [[e:quito|Quito]] became renowned for the [[e:quito-school|Quito School]] of painting and sculpture and for churches such as [[e:church-of-the-society-of-jesus-quito|La Compañía]]. The [[e:rebellion-of-the-barrios|Rebellion of the Barrios]] in 1765 protested new taxes.

Real power lay with the [[e:yang-dipertuan-muda|Yang Dipertuan Muda]], [[e:bugis|Bugis]] viceroys based on [[e:penyengat|Penyengat]] island. Gambier and [[e:pepper|pepper]] planted by Chinese settlers on Bintan funded the court. Penyengat became a cradle of Malay letters, where [[e:raja-ali-haji|Raja Ali Haji]] wrote the [[e:gurindam-dua-belas|Gurindam Dua Belas]] and an early Malay grammar, laying foundations for standard Malay.

With sea otters depleted and [[e:russia|Russia]] fearing it could not defend [[e:alaska|Alaska]] against [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] after the Crimean War, the territory was sold to the [[s:united-states|United States]] in 1867 for $7.2 million. The [[e:russian-orthodox-church|Russian Orthodox Church]] remains a lasting legacy in Alaska.
Egypt as the richest province of the Roman and Byzantine empires, the granary of Rome and a cradle of Christian monasticism.

The [[e:palestine-liberation-organization|Palestine Liberation Organization]], founded in 1964 and led from 1969 by [[e:yasser-arafat|Yasser Arafat]], came to embody Palestinian nationhood after the [[e:nakba|Nakba]] of 1948 had scattered much of the Arab population of [[s:mandatory-palestine|Mandatory Palestine]]. On 15 November 1988 the PLO declared the State of Palestine in Algiers, claiming the West Bank, Gaza and East Jerusalem, territories held by Israel since the [[e:six-day-war|Six-Day War]].
The short-lived East Javanese kingdom of Ken Arok and Kertanegara, which defied Kublai Khan and paved the way for Majapahit.

Little is known of its internal life. It was a Hurrian-influenced hill kingdom with fortified towns controlling trade in metals, [[e:timber|timber]] and horses. [[e:shulgi|Shulgi]] of the [[s:neo-sumerian-empire|Neo-Sumerian Empire]] boasted of destroying Simurrum several times. A local king, [[e:iddin-sin|Iddin-Sin]], and his son Zabazuna left Akkadian inscriptions and a rock relief celebrating their victories, revealing a brief period of independent power around 2000 BCE.

The [[s:state-of-chu|State of Chu]] annexed Qi in 445 BCE as it expanded into the lands between the Huai and the [[e:yellow-river|Yellow River]]. Its main legacy is symbolic: it embodied the Zhou practice of preserving defeated royal lines, and its name survives in the Chinese idiom for needless anxiety.
The British colony at Freetown, founded as a home for freed slaves, which became the base of the anti-slave-trade squadron and the cradle of Krio culture.

The Sawants ruled a coastal and hilly territory of [[e:rice|rice]], coconut and cashew. Their state was long troubled by piracy disputes and internal revolts, and British officers administered it for periods in the 19th century. The court fostered crafts such as lacquered wooden toys and [[e:ganjifa|Ganjifa]] playing cards.
A Singh Deo-ruled state of the Chota Nagpur plateau, cradle of the masked Seraikela style of Chhau dance.
The self-governing foreign enclave at the heart of Shanghai, run by a council of foreign ratepayers, which made the city China's commercial capital.

The reth was a sacred king, believed to embody the spirit of [[e:nyikang|Nyikang]]; his health was linked to the wellbeing of the land, a case made famous by [[e:james-frazer|James Frazer]] and [[e:e-e-evans-pritchard|E. E. Evans-Pritchard]]. Settlements were dense along the river, living from [[e:sorghum|sorghum]], [[e:cattle|cattle]] and fishing. [[e:shilluk-people|Shilluk]] canoe fleets raided as far north as the [[s:funj-sultanate|Funj Sultanate]].

Han held a central but exposed position on the routes from [[e:qin-dynasty|Qin]] to the eastern plain. Under Marquis Zhao the minister [[e:shen-buhai|Shen Buhai]] developed methods for controlling officials, and Han's [[e:crossbow|crossbows]] and swords were renowned. Its prince [[e:han-fei|Han Fei]] wrote the classic statement of [[e:legalism|Legalism]]. Han's attempt to exhaust Qin by having the engineer [[s:state-of-zheng|Zheng]] [[e:guo-state|Guo]] build a canal backfired by enriching Qin.
